10210-wolves-of-the-sea-being-a-tale-of-:
Randall Parrish published this sea novel in 1918, setting it in the days of the early American colonies. Its narrator, Geoffry Carlyle, is a seaman who tells his own story in the first person, looking back on youth, danger, and a woman he never forgot. The tale moves from English jails and forced labor to ships off Virginia and the Chesapeake.

Carlyle is sent into servitude, held on a prison ship, and then drawn aboard the pirate craft Namur, where Dorothy Fairfax is also at risk. Mutiny, murder, escape in an open boat, a slaver, and a hunt for treasure follow, chapter by chapter. Readers get a fast, old-style adventure of loyalty, daring, and love at sea.
23691-archeological-expedition-to-arizon:
Jesse Walter Fewkes wrote this report of his 1895 expedition to Arizona for the Bureau of American Ethnology. It surveys ancient ruins in two regions: the Verde Valley and Tusayan, the Hopi country. Fewkes maps, measures, and classifies what he finds, and sets down the stories told about each place.

Verde Valley sites include Montezuma Well, the cliff houses of the Red-rocks, Palatki, and Honanki, with the objects found there. In Tusayan he treats the Middle Mesa and East Mesa ruins, the legend of Awatobi's destruction, and the great pueblo of Sikyatki. Pottery, stone tools, bone objects, shrines, and prayer-sticks all get careful chapters, making this a foundation record of Southwest archaeology.
24583-langstroth-on-the-hive-and-the-hon:
The Reverend L. L. Langstroth wrote this bee-keeper's manual, published at Northampton by Hopkins, Bridgman. Its title page shows the queen, the worker, and the drone, with bees surrounding their queen as she rests upon the comb. Langstroth, the inventor of the movable-frame hive, wrote for keepers who wanted healthy bees and good honey.

Chapters cover the hive, the honey-bee's life, swarming, feeding, and the care of colonies through the seasons. Langstroth quotes Shakespeare on bees teaching order to a peopled kingdom. His manual remains the founding book of modern beekeeping, practical, clear, and still read by keepers today.
24956-live-to-be-useful-or-the-story-of-:
Thomas Nelson and Sons' 1913 story follows Annie Lee, a girl crippled from her eighth summer who endures five years of pain with devout cheerfulness. Rather than sinking into self-pity, Annie consoles her parents and turns her sickroom into a place of comfort for others. Her faith steadies the household, and her patience becomes a quiet lesson for everyone around her.

Irish nurse Annorah tends Annie with warmth and plain sense, while Biddy Dillon's lame boy Phelim finds in Annie a fellow sufferer who understands him. A priest disputing with Annorah adds a note of doctrinal debate to the household scenes. The book's moral is in its title: usefulness, not health or fortune, gives a life its worth.
25200-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-volum:
The Index to volume 17 of Chambers's Edinburgh Journal covers numbers 418 to 443, from January to June 1852. William and Robert Chambers conducted the journal from London and Edinburgh, and this volume's index maps every article to its page.

Entries range from familiar sketches and moral essays to notes on Liberia, Nantucket sea-kings, South African reptiles, and the thinness of a soap bubble. A transcriber's cross-reference ties each issue number to its dates and pages. The index itself is a useful guide to what a popular Victorian weekly offered its readers.
britannica-1911-ainu:
Ainu, a people of Japan's northernmost islands, are treated at length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Their name means man in their own tongue. Little is known for certain about their earliest history. Careful research, the entry argues, shows they were immigrants rather than Japan's first inhabitants, reaching Yezo by way of the Kurile islands.

Crossing the Tsugaru strait, the Ainu once settled much of Japan's main island, displacing a small pit-dwelling people they called koro-pok-guru. The Japanese, arriving from the south and west, later drove the Ainu north into Yezo, the Kuriles, and southern Sakhalin. The entry then covers their beliefs, including a supreme Creator alongside sun, moon, water, and mountain gods. It also pictures their world resting on a great fish whose movements cause earthquakes, a fancy likely borrowed from the Japanese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-laws-of-m:
Ancient India's sacred law book, the Manava Dharma-sastra, is introduced here under its English name, the Laws of Manu. Brahmins revere it highly and credit it with divine origin and remote antiquity. Its reputed author, Manu, survived the Flood as father of humanity and now enjoys in heaven the rank of an all-knowing deity.

Ten great sages approached Manu and asked him to declare the sacred laws of the castes. He answered by having Bhrigu, carefully taught in the metrical institutes, deliver the instruction. So the work claims to be Manu's dictation through Bhrigu, learned in turn from self-existent Brahma. Contents, castes, duties, and penalties follow in outline.

podcast-tuckercarlson-XS7itdfgNnU:
Tucker Carlson questions former governor Mike Huckabee in a tense interview about the United States and Israel. The episode title calls the bond between the two lands toxic. Huckabee is a strong backer of Israel, which sets up a sharp clash with his host.

Carlson presses Huckabee on foreign aid, war, and how faith shapes views of Israel. Huckabee defends the bond and his own role in it. The heat in the room is the point of the episode. Listeners can hear two men on the same broad side of politics split hard over one country and what America owes it.
